questions.stem: In the particle model of light, a photon is:
options: a discrete packet of electromagnetic energy, with energy E = hf
a small charged particle that carries light energy from a source
a wave of any energy, which depends on the brightness of the light
an electron released from a metal surface when light strikes it
questions.explanation: Light energy comes in discrete quanta called photons, each with energy E = hf, so the energy depends only on frequency. Photons have no charge. An electron released from a metal by light is a photoelectron, not a photon.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon of light with a wavelength of 500 nm?
questions.explanation: E = hc/λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/5.00 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, about 2.5 eV. Multiplying h by λ instead of dividing gives 3.3 × 10⁻⁴⁰ J, leaving the wavelength in nanometres gives 4.0 × 10⁻²⁸ J, and h/λ without c gives 1.3 × 10⁻²⁷.

questions.stem: A photon has an energy of 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its frequency?
options: 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz
questions.explanation: f = E/h = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ ≈ 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz, in the violet part of the spectrum. Dividing h by E gives the reciprocal, 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁵ Hz, and multiplying gives 3.3 × 10⁻⁵² Hz.

questions.stem: How does the energy of a single photon change if the wavelength of the light is doubled?
options: It stays the same
It halves
It doubles
It quarters
questions.explanation: E = hc/λ, so photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength. Doubling λ halves the frequency and halves the energy of each photon.

questions.stem: A 5.0 mW laser emits light of wavelength 633 nm. About how many photons does it emit each second?
questions.explanation: Each photon has E = hc/λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/6.33 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 3.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The number per second is the power divided by the photon energy: 5.0 × 10⁻³/3.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 1.6 × 10¹⁶. Using 5.0 W instead of 5.0 mW gives 1.6 × 10¹⁹.

questions.stem: Two lamps emit the same power. One emits only red light and the other only blue light. Which statement is correct?
options: Both emit the same number of photons per second, because their powers are the same
The red lamp emits fewer photons per second, because red light has a lower intensity
The red lamp emits more photons per second, because each red photon carries less energy
The blue lamp emits more photons per second, because each blue photon carries more energy
questions.explanation: Power is the number of photons per second multiplied by the energy of each photon. Red light has a lower frequency, so each photon has less energy, and the red lamp must emit more photons each second to deliver the same power.

questions.stem: How is the temperature of an object related to the motion of its particles?
options: Higher temperature means the particles move more slowly but have a greater mass
Temperature measures the potential energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy
Higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy and a wider energy spread
Higher temperature means every particle has exactly the same, larger kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. The particles have a range of energies, and at higher temperature the average rises and the distribution spreads to higher energies. Particles never all share one identical energy.

questions.stem: Why does every object emit electromagnetic radiation that depends on its temperature?
options: Only objects that glow visibly emit radiation; cold objects emit none at all
Thermal motion accelerates its charges, and accelerating charges radiate
Its atoms are heated until they become radioactive and then emit gamma rays
It reflects the radiation that falls on it, more strongly when it is hot
questions.explanation: The charged particles in matter jiggle with thermal energy, and accelerating charges emit electromagnetic radiation. Hotter objects have more energetic motion, so they radiate more and at higher frequencies. Even cool objects emit, mainly in the infrared.

questions.stem: A theoretical black body is:
options: an object that emits radiation only at one wavelength, set by its temperature
a perfect absorber and a perfect emitter of radiation at all wavelengths
an object that absorbs all radiation but never emits any radiation
an object that reflects all radiation and so looks perfectly black
questions.explanation: A black body absorbs all radiation falling on it, reflecting none, and it is also the best possible emitter at every temperature. Its emission spectrum depends only on its temperature. A good absorber is always a good emitter.

questions.stem: Why is a small hole in the wall of a hollow cavity a good model of a black body?
options: The cavity walls are perfect mirrors, so all incoming radiation is sent straight back out
The hole is too small for any radiation to enter it, so nothing is reflected back out
Radiation entering the hole is reflected inside until absorbed, so almost none escapes
The hole lets radiation pass straight through the cavity without being absorbed at all
questions.explanation: Any radiation entering the hole bounces around inside and is absorbed by the walls before it can find its way back out, so the hole absorbs nearly everything. When the cavity is heated, the radiation coming out of the hole has a black-body spectrum set by the wall temperature.

questions.stem: As the temperature of a black body increases, how does its radiation curve change?
options: The peak moves to shorter wavelengths but the total energy emitted decreases
The peak stays at the same wavelength but the whole curve becomes taller
The peak moves to shorter wavelengths and the curve rises at every wavelength
The peak moves to longer wavelengths and the curve gets higher at every wavelength
questions.explanation: A hotter black body emits more radiation at every wavelength, so its whole curve lies above that of a cooler one, and its peak shifts to shorter wavelengths by Wien's law. That is why a heated metal glows red, then orange, then white as it gets hotter.

questions.stem: Using Wien's law, λmax = b/T, at what wavelength does the radiation from the Sun's surface, at about 5800 K, peak?
options: 50 nm
500 nm
questions.explanation: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³/5800 ≈ 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, or 500 nm, in the visible range. Multiplying b by T instead of dividing gives 17 m, and slips with the power of ten give 50 nm.

questions.stem: A person's skin is at about 310 K. At what wavelength does its thermal radiation peak?
options: 930 nm, in the visible
0.93 m, in the radio band
9.3 µm, in the infrared
93 nm, in the ultraviolet
questions.explanation: λmax = b/T = 2.898 × 10⁻³/310 ≈ 9.3 × 10⁻⁶ m, about 9.3 µm. This is in the infrared, which is why thermal cameras can detect people in the dark. The other values come from slips with powers of ten.

questions.stem: A star's radiation peaks at a wavelength of 290 nm. What is its surface temperature?
questions.explanation: T = b/λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³/2.90 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁴ K, so the star is hotter than the Sun and looks blue-white. Leaving the wavelength in nanometres gives 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ K, and multiplying instead of dividing gives 8.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ K.

questions.stem: What was the ultraviolet catastrophe?
options: Experiments showed that black bodies emit no ultraviolet radiation at any temperature
Classical physics predicted black-body intensity rising without limit at short wavelengths
Early ultraviolet lamps released far more energy than classical physics said they could
Ultraviolet light was found to travel faster than visible light does in a vacuum
questions.explanation: Classical theory, which let the energy of the radiation take any value, predicted that the intensity emitted by a black body would keep rising as wavelength decreased, giving infinite total energy. Measured curves rise to a peak and then fall to zero at short wavelengths. The clash showed the classical model was wrong.

questions.stem: How did Planck's proposal that energy is quantised, E = hf, resolve the conflict over black-body radiation?
options: It allowed energy to take any value, so the predicted curve could be adjusted to match the data
It showed that black bodies emit only one frequency, which explains why the curve has a peak
It showed that ultraviolet radiation is absorbed by the air, so it never reaches detectors
High-frequency quanta need so much energy that few are emitted, so the curve falls at short wavelengths
questions.explanation: If energy can only be emitted in quanta of hf, then high-frequency quanta are large compared with the thermal energy available, so few are emitted. This cuts off the curve at short wavelengths and gives curves that match experiment. The episode showed that a theory must be revised when its predictions disagree with observation.

questions.stem: In the photoelectric effect:
options: a metal surface becomes positively charged when it is struck by fast-moving protons
electrons leave a metal surface when light above a threshold frequency falls on it
light is emitted from a metal surface when a current of electrons passes through it
electrons are emitted from a metal surface whenever it is heated to a high temperature
questions.explanation: Photons with enough energy can each give an electron enough energy to escape the metal. Below a threshold frequency no electrons are emitted, however bright the light. Emission caused by heating is thermionic emission, a different effect.

questions.stem: The work function φ of a metal is:
options: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from its surface
the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons emitted from its surface
the energy of the photons that strike the surface of the metal
the voltage needed to make a current flow through the metal
questions.explanation: The work function is the least energy needed to free an electron from the metal's surface. A photon's energy hf goes first into overcoming φ, and what is left can become the electron's kinetic energy, so K_max = hf − φ.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 400 nm, with photons of energy 3.10 eV, falls on a metal with a work function of 2.30 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons?
questions.explanation: K_max = hf − φ = 3.10 − 2.30 = 0.80 eV, by conservation of energy. Adding the work function instead of subtracting gives 5.40 eV, which would create energy from nothing.

questions.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, the photocurrent is stopped by a reverse voltage of 0.80 V. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in joules?
questions.explanation: K_max = qV₀ = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.80 ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The stopping voltage tells us the most energetic electrons have 0.80 eV. Dividing the voltage by the charge gives 5.0 × 10¹⁸, which is not an energy.

questions.stem: A metal has a work function of 2.30 eV. What is its threshold frequency?
options: 3.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz
5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz
3.5 × 10³³ Hz
1.8 × 10¹⁵ Hz
questions.explanation: At the threshold frequency the photon energy just equals the work function. φ = 2.30 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 3.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so f₀ = φ/h = 3.68 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ ≈ 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Forgetting to convert electronvolts to joules gives 3.5 × 10³³ Hz.

questions.stem: Light above the threshold frequency falls on a metal. The intensity is doubled while the frequency stays the same. What happens?
options: Twice as many photoelectrons are emitted, with the same maximum kinetic energy
The same number of photoelectrons are emitted, with twice the maximum kinetic energy
Twice as many photoelectrons are emitted, each with twice the kinetic energy
No change, because only frequency affects the photoelectric effect
questions.explanation: Doubling the intensity at the same frequency doubles the number of photons per second, so twice as many electrons are released and the current doubles. Each photon still has energy hf, so K_max = hf − φ is unchanged.

questions.stem: Very bright red light shines on a metal but no electrons are emitted. Dim ultraviolet light on the same metal does release electrons. How does the quantum model explain this?
options: Each red photon has less energy than the work function; each UV photon has more
Red light is absorbed by the air before it reaches the surface of the metal
Bright light heats the metal so much that the electrons are held more tightly
Ultraviolet light is more intense than red light, even when it looks dimmer
questions.explanation: One photon gives its energy to one electron. If hf is below the work function, no electron can escape, however many photons arrive. UV photons have higher frequency and enough energy individually. The wave model predicted that bright light of any frequency would eventually release electrons, which is not observed.

questions.stem: Graphs of maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against light frequency are drawn for two different metals. How do the two lines compare?
options: They are parallel to the frequency axis, because K_max does not depend on frequency
They are parallel, with gradient h, but cross the frequency axis at different threshold frequencies
They have different gradients, equal to each metal's work function, but share one threshold frequency
They meet at the origin, with steeper gradients for metals that have larger work functions
questions.explanation: K_max = hf − φ is a straight line with gradient h, the same for every metal. The frequency-axis intercept is the threshold frequency f₀ = φ/h, and the extended line meets the energy axis at −φ, so a metal with a larger work function has a line shifted to the right.

questions.stem: On a graph of K_max against frequency for a photoelectric experiment, what does the gradient give?
options: Planck's constant, h
The work function, φ
The threshold frequency, f₀
The stopping voltage, V₀
questions.explanation: Comparing K_max = hf − φ with y = mx + c, the gradient is h. The work function is found from the magnitude of the vertical intercept, and the threshold frequency from where the line crosses the frequency axis.

questions.stem: Which observation of the photoelectric effect supports the quantum model of light rather than the wave model?
options: Electrons are emitted with no measurable delay, even in very dim light
More electrons are emitted when the light is made brighter at the same frequency
Emitted electrons have a range of kinetic energies, up to a fixed maximum
The photocurrent stops when a large enough reverse voltage is applied
questions.explanation: The wave model predicted that in dim light an electron would need time to absorb enough energy to escape. In fact, emission begins immediately, because one photon delivers all its energy to one electron at once. A brighter beam giving more electrons fits both models.

questions.stem: Thermionic emission is the release of electrons from a metal surface:
options: when the metal is heated, giving electrons enough energy to escape
when light above the threshold frequency falls on the metal surface
when the metal is cooled, so the electrons are less tightly bound
when the metal is placed in a strong, steady magnetic field
questions.explanation: Heating a metal gives some of its electrons enough kinetic energy to overcome the work function and escape, as in the heated cathode of an electron gun. Release by light is the photoelectric effect.

questions.stem: In a thermionic emission experiment, a reverse voltage of 1.5 V just stops the most energetic electrons from a hot filament reaching the collector. What is their maximum kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: The reverse voltage does work qV₀ against each electron, so K_max = qV₀ = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.5 ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (1.5 eV). Dividing 1.5 by the charge gives 9.4 × 10¹⁸, which is not an energy.

questions.stem: How does a photovoltaic (solar) cell use the photoelectric effect?
options: Photons are stored in the cell and released later as light whenever a current is needed
Photons push the cell's magnets around, inducing a current in a coil of wire
Photons free electrons in a semiconductor, and the junction drives them round a circuit
Photons heat the cell, and the heat boils water that turns a small turbine and generator
questions.explanation: In a solar cell, photons with enough energy free electrons in the semiconductor (an internal photoelectric effect). An electric field built into the junction separates the freed charges, producing a voltage and driving a current through an external circuit.

questions.stem: Which device, apart from a solar cell, relies on the photoelectric effect?
options: An electric kettle that heats water using a coil
A compass that points north in Earth's field
A light sensor that switches the street lights on at dusk
A transformer that steps down the mains voltage
questions.explanation: Photodiodes and phototubes in light sensors produce a current that depends on the light falling on them, so a circuit can switch lights on when daylight fades. Transformers and compasses rely on electromagnetism, and kettles on resistive heating.

questions.stem: The work function of zinc is about 4.3 eV. Will visible light, with photon energies of about 1.8 to 3.1 eV, eject electrons from zinc?
options: No, because each visible photon has less energy than φ
Yes, because bright enough visible light will always eject electrons
Yes, because the energies of two photons can add to exceed 4.3 eV
No, because zinc reflects all visible light from its surface
questions.explanation: Each photon interacts with a single electron, so the photon energy must be at least 4.3 eV. Visible photons fall short, so ultraviolet light is needed for zinc. Increasing brightness adds more photons but does not raise the energy of each one.

questions.stem: Light with photons of energy 3.10 eV falls on two metals. Metal X has a work function of 2.3 eV and metal Y has a work function of 2.9 eV. What stopping voltages are needed?
options: 3.1 V for both metals
0.8 V for X and 0.2 V for Y
2.3 V for X and 2.9 V for Y
0.2 V for X and 0.8 V for Y
questions.explanation: K_max = hf − φ gives 0.8 eV for X and 0.2 eV for Y, and since K_max = qV₀, the stopping voltages are 0.8 V and 0.2 V. The metal with the larger work function needs the smaller stopping voltage. The work function itself is not the stopping voltage.

questions.stem: What is the value of 1 electronvolt in joules?
questions.explanation: One electronvolt is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through 1 V: E = qV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 1 V. The value 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ is Planck's constant in J s, and 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ is the electron's mass in kilograms.

questions.stem: How do observations of the photoelectric effect validate predictions about the quantum nature of light?
options: They show that electrons are emitted only after a delay, as the quantum model predicts
They show interference patterns in the emitted electrons, as E = hf predicts
They show a threshold frequency and K_max rising linearly with f, as E = hf predicts
They show that brighter light gives faster electrons, as the quantum model predicts
questions.explanation: If light comes in photons of energy hf, there should be a threshold frequency below which no electrons escape, and K_max should rise linearly with frequency with gradient h. Experiments, notably Millikan's careful measurements, confirmed both predictions. Brightness affects the number of electrons, not their energy.

questions.stem: What happens to the energy of each photon when the frequency of light is increased?
options: It stays the same, because all photons are identical
It increases in proportion to the square of the frequency
It increases in proportion to the frequency
It decreases in proportion to the frequency
questions.explanation: E = hf, so photon energy is directly proportional to frequency. Doubling the frequency doubles the energy of each photon. Photons of different frequencies carry different energies.

questions.stem: Which symbol in K_max = hf − φ stands for Planck's constant, and what is its value?
questions.explanation: Planck's constant h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s links a photon's energy to its frequency. φ is the work function, 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the elementary charge in coulombs, and 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K is Wien's constant.

questions.stem: A metal is lit with light below its threshold frequency. The light is made ten times brighter. What happens?
options: Electrons are emitted with low energy
Still no electrons are emitted
Electrons are emitted after a delay
Ten times as many electrons are emitted
questions.explanation: Below the threshold frequency each photon has less energy than the work function, so no single photon can free an electron. Brighter light only sends more of these low-energy photons. The wave model predicted emission after a delay, but none is observed.
